title: Read to the dying
hookLine: the text is read aloud to the dying and the dead

lines: READ TO THE ONE WHO IS DYING.
cards: A small room, the lamps low. Someone has just died, or is very close to it.
Beside the bed sits a monk, or a family friend who knows how, with a long, narrow book on their knees: loose pages printed in Tibetan, held between two boards. And they are reading out loud.
Not to the family, though the family hears it. Not to themselves. They are reading to the person who is dying, and they will keep reading after the breathing stops.
That is what this book was made for.

teach.b: The book is the Bardo Thodol, which means liberation through hearing in the in-between. Hearing: the whole name rests on it. It isn't mainly a book for scholars to study at a desk.

teach.h: SPOKEN TO THE ONE WHO DIED.
teach.b: It is a book to be spoken into someone's ear. The reader addresses the one who has died by name, the way a guide talks to a traveler on a dark road: this is the clear light, recognize it.

These visions are your own mind; don't be afraid. Tradition holds that awareness goes on hearing after the body has gone quiet, so the reading goes on too, through the days of the in-between. Where did it come from?
Tibetan tradition says Padmasambhava taught it and hid it as a treasure, and that a treasure-revealer, Karma Lingpa, brought it to light long afterward. And it isn't only for the dead.

teach.h: READ IN LIFE, HEARD AT THE END.
teach.b: Some teachers say it's meant to be heard long before the end, read in life, so the words are already familiar when they're needed most.
It shapes the living in the room too: someone sitting by a deathbed, with nothing to fix, is given something to do with their voice.
Look back across this week: the great seal and the great perfection, the teacher face to face, the in-between, the clear light, the two walls of visions.
All of it, in the end, carried by a human voice reading aloud. And if a loss is heavy on you right now and you feel in danger, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency help.

how: In Tibetan communities, a lama, monk or trained friend may read the Bardo Thodol aloud beside someone who is dying and continue reading after death, speaking directly to the one who has died through the days of the in-between.

games.q: what does “read to the dying” mean?
o: reading the Bardo Thodol aloud to the dying and the dead
writing goodbye letters to someone before they die
reading a will aloud to the family after a death

taught and hid it, tradition says

the reading continues after the breathing stops

games.q: you're sitting beside a friend who has just died. you've been given the book. who do you read it to?
o: your friend who has died, speaking to them directly.
games.why: the reader speaks to the one who has died, by name, like a guide on a dark road, though everyone in the room hears it too.

practice: Find something kind to read: a verse from the Dhammapada, a few lines from a book you love, a letter someone once wrote you.
Read it aloud, slowly, as if someone you care about were sitting beside you and needed to hear it, letting each line land before you go on. If you have someone in mind, let it be for them.

wordCard.voice: Read to the dying. The Tibetan practice of speaking the Bardo Thodol aloud to the one who is dying, and to the one who has died. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan bar do thos grol: the in-between, hearing, liberation. Liberation through hearing in the in-between.

carryVoice: Your line: read aloud. A voice can keep someone company on a dark road. That closes the week.
